subject: nlp
title: Practice quiz
description: The lecturer's practice quiz (all sections, lectures 1–8), transcribed word for word. Only the order of questions and options is randomised. Answers are unofficial: the paper has no memo.
negativeMarkingNote: Not stated on the practice paper: the real Moodle quiz uses negative marking on MCQ questions, so picking all right and wrong answers on a question results in a mark of 0.
transcriptionNotes: Question and option text is copied exactly from the PDF, including mark annotations such as '(1 Mark)', odd quotation marks and typos ('how they combined', 'very imbalance', 'which adjust', 'how many words probable words'). Line breaks from the PDF layout are removed. Sections 5 and 6 give no marks on the paper, so each question is worth 1. The paper doesn't mention negative marking; it's enabled on the multi-select questions to match the real Moodle quiz. Option 4.3(e) is a True/False statement inside a multi-select question on the original, and is kept as is. Answers and explanations are written by Claude, not the lecturer.

questions.question: Syntax is the rule system of how to combine: (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: Syntax governs how words combine into phrases and sentences. Combining morphemes into words is morphology.

questions.question: The difference between a root and stem word is: (1 Mark)
choices: The stem is the root word with derivational affixes
They are completely different words in meaning
The stem is the root word with inflectable affixes
Root word is a synonym but different word to the stem
questions.explanation: The root is the core morpheme (e.g. 'teach'). A stem is the root plus any derivational affixes (e.g. 'teacher'); inflectional affixes are then added to the stem ('teachers').
questions.keyDispute: No official key. Option (c) is the main distractor: inflectional affixes attach TO a stem, they don't create one.

questions.question: True or False, when we reference “semantics” we are referring to the meaning of words and how they combined to form meaningful sentences. (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: Semantics is the study of meaning: of words and of how their meanings combine into sentence meaning.

questions.question: Which of the following are true? (4 Marks)
choices: Word2Vec performs negative sampling as a means to speed up training.
Word2Vec embeddings are more useful for downstream tasks than 1-hot representations on words which aren’t in the vocabulary
Intrinsic evaluation of word embeddings evaluates how well the word vectors perform on a downstream task
Simple tokenization schemes are particularly good for languages with rich morphology
questions.explanation: (a) True: negative sampling replaces the full softmax over the vocabulary with a few sampled negatives. (b) False: Word2Vec has no vector for an out-of-vocabulary word either, so it is no better there. (c) False: that describes extrinsic evaluation; intrinsic evaluation tests the vectors directly (similarity, analogies). (d) False: rich morphology makes simple (whitespace) tokenization produce huge, sparse vocabularies.
questions.keyDispute: No official key. (b) is the debatable one; it reads as a trick about out-of-vocabulary words.

questions.question: Complete the sentence: ”The problem with using the cosine distance to measure word similarity of vector representations is...” (1 mark)
choices: the cosine distance does not account for the magnitude of the vectors (only the angle between them)
the cosine distance is longer if words have higher frequencies
the cosine distance is longer if words have higher values
the cosine distance is 0 when vectors are orthogonal
questions.explanation: Cosine only compares direction; any information carried by vector length (e.g. frequency or confidence) is ignored. Normalising by length is exactly what stops it from growing with frequency or magnitude.

questions.question: What function is typically used to get the probability distribution over classes, after the linear layer? Please write the name of the function only without spaces at the beginning and end of the name. (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Softmax turns the linear layer's scores (logits) into a probability distribution: $\frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j)}$. For two classes a sigmoid does the same job.

questions.question: True or False, the Bag-of-Words (count based features) is an example of a neural method of feature extraction. (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: Bag-of-Words is a manual, count-based feature: no learning is involved. Neural methods learn features (e.g. embeddings + CNN/RNN).

questions.question: Laplace smoothing is used in case: (1 Mark)
choices: Too many stop words appear in the training data.
An unseen word appears during inference.
The class labels are very imbalance.
questions.explanation: Without smoothing, a word never seen with a class has count 0, so P(word|class) = 0 and the whole product becomes 0. Adding $\delta$ to every count prevents that.

questions.question: True or False, a support vector machine (SVM) is a discriminative model similar to logistic regression (can be used for classification). (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: Like logistic regression, an SVM models the decision boundary between classes directly rather than how the data is generated (Naive Bayes is generative).

questions.question: True or False, CNNs for NLP represent time spatially while RNNs do not. (1 Mark. * this is probably on the more difficult side and might require some thinking)
questions.explanation: A CNN lays the sequence out as positions and slides filters across them, so order becomes a spatial axis. An RNN represents order temporally: step $t$ depends on step $t-1$. (Tutorial 4.3 asks you to explain exactly this.)

questions.question: True or False, an embedding layer is functionally equivalent to a linear layer (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: An embedding lookup is a linear layer (without bias) applied to a one-hot vector: multiplying a one-hot vector by the weight matrix just selects one row. The lookup is simply the efficient way to do it.
questions.keyDispute: No official key. 'Functionally equivalent' assumes a one-hot input and no bias.

questions.question: True or False, when using an N-gram language model Backoff aims to fix the problem that, as N becomes larger, individual inputs (the N-grams) become more rare (1 Mark)
questions.explanation: Long N-grams are sparse, so many have zero counts. Backoff falls back to shorter contexts (trigram → bigram → unigram) when the longer one hasn't been seen.

questions.question: Please select the answers that are true statements about text generation strategies (5 Marks)
choices: Temperature is a hyper-parameter added to the softmax of a neural language model
By changing the temperature we aim to control the coherence-diversity trade-off in neural language models
Higher temperatures result in more coherent text
Lower temperatures result in more coherent text
True or False, Nucleus sampling (Top-p sampling) is an adaptive method of sampling which adjust how many words could be chosen from based on how many words probable words there are
questions.explanation: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax (a hyperparameter). $\tau < 1$ sharpens the distribution: more coherent, less diverse. $\tau > 1$ flattens it: more diverse, less coherent. Top-p adapts the candidate set to the distribution (2 words for 'the light was…', many for 'the dress colour was…').

questions.question: Which of the statements is true about the structure of Seq2Seq Models:
choices: The encoder processes the previous history
The decoder processes the source text
The encoder provides word embeddings for the decoder
The decoder processes the previous history
questions.explanation: The encoder reads the source; the decoder processes the previous target history (what it has already generated) and predicts the next token. The encoder passes a source representation, not word embeddings.

questions.question: Which one of the following does the final encoder state of an RNN represent?
choices: The semantic embedding of the last word it is shown
The semantic embedding of the entire sentence with a bias towards the last word it is shown
The semantic embedding of the entire sentence with no positional bias
The semantic embedding of the entire sentence with a bias towards the first word it is shown
questions.explanation: It summarises the whole sentence, but recent tokens dominate because earlier ones fade through repeated recurrent updates. This bottleneck is what motivates attention.

questions.question: True or False: Seq2Seq models predict next words in a sentence.
questions.explanation: The decoder is a conditional language model: it predicts the next target token given the previous target tokens and the source.

questions.question: True or False: The use of Softmax in the attention calculation makes the attention sparse.
questions.explanation: In lecture 6 the lecturer said: 'you're going to have this really sparse set of attention weights. They may not be exactly zero, but they're going to all be really close to zero except for hopefully one or two.' Softmax pushes most weights towards 0 and concentrates on a few tokens.
questions.keyDispute: Toss-up, no official key. Strictly, softmax never outputs exact zeros, so it is not sparse in the mathematical sense (sparsemax would be), which would make the answer False. True is chosen here because of how the lecturer described it in class.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a common score function used within attention (not necessarily only self attention in Transformers):
questions.explanation: The three score functions are dot-product, bilinear and MLP. Softmax turns the scores into weights; it isn't a score function. (Same idea as 2025 Quiz 2, Q1.)

questions.question: True or False: It is possible to have a useful transformer model even if we remove the encoder part of the network.
questions.explanation: Decoder-only Transformers (the GPT family) drop the encoder and cross-attention and work as large left-to-right language models.

questions.question: Which of the following is not one of the tokens that gets replaced to form the training object for a BERT model:
questions.explanation: BERT picks 15% of tokens; of those, 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% stay unchanged. Synonyms are never used.

questions.question: True or False: The ELMo Model includes context in the token representations directly, unlike other tokenisers such as BPE or SentencePiece.
questions.explanation: ELMo's representations come from a bidirectional LSTM language model, so the same word gets a different vector in different sentences. BPE/SentencePiece only segment text; they produce no contextual vectors.

questions.question: True or False: The ELMo Model is not an “open-vocabulary” tokenisation model.
questions.explanation: ELMo builds word representations from characters (character-level CNN + highway layers), so it can represent any word, including unseen ones. It IS open-vocabulary, so the statement is False.
